title: OLM Interneurons
intro: Oriens-lacunosum moleculare (OLM) cells are somatostatin-expressing interneurons of the hippocampus. Their somata and dendrites sit in stratum oriens, below the CA1 pyramidal layer, and their axon climbs all the way to stratum lacunosum-moleculare, where it inhibits the distal tufts of pyramidal cells exactly where entorhinal input arrives. They are the hippocampal counterpart of cortical Martinotti cells, and their slow intrinsic rhythm made them a central element in models of theta oscillations.

items: Morphology: horizontally oriented dendrites in stratum oriens, an axon that crosses the pyramidal and radiatum layers and branches densely in stratum lacunosum-moleculare.
Markers: somatostatin, often mGluR1a; many express the nicotinic α2 receptor (Chrna2), which gives genetic access in mice (Leao et al. 2012).

Firing: spontaneous, regular firing at theta-range frequencies (about 4 to 10 Hz) driven by a strong h-current and persistent sodium current; prominent sag on hyperpolarisation and rebound spikes (Maccaferri & McBain 1996).

Inputs: excitation mostly from local CA1 pyramidal cells (feedback), through facilitating synapses, plus septal cholinergic and GABAergic input; inhibition from VIP/calretinin interneuron-selective cells.

Outputs: slow-ish GABA-A inhibition of pyramidal cell tufts; they also inhibit interneurons in stratum radiatum that themselves inhibit pyramidal cells, so they can disinhibit Schaffer collateral input (Leao et al. 2012).
In vivo timing: OLM cells fire at the trough of theta in CA1 and are silent during sharp-wave ripples (Klausberger et al. 2003).

Pathway gating: by inhibiting the entorhinal input zone and disinhibiting the CA3 input zone, OLM cells shift CA1's balance from 'current sensory input' toward 'memory recall from CA3' (Leao et al. 2012).
Theta rhythm: their intrinsic theta-rate firing and slow inhibition make them candidate pacemakers or phase-setters for theta.
Plasticity control: by controlling distal dendritic depolarisation, they influence plateau potentials and plasticity in CA1 pyramidal cells.

Gloveli, Kopell and colleagues: in the models of Rotstein et al. (2005), Gloveli et al. (2005) and Tort et al. (2007), O-LM cells with an h-current and slow GABA-A synapses interact with fast-spiking basket cells and pyramidal cells to produce nested theta and gamma rhythms. The O-LM cell's slow inhibition sets the theta period, the basket cell's fast inhibition sets gamma.

Saraga et al. (2003): a multi-compartment OLM model with dendritic h-current and its theta resonance; Sekulic and Skinner (2017) studied OLM models with experimentally constrained h-channel distributions.
Point models: two-compartment or single-compartment HH models with I_h and I_NaP; Izhikevich parameters for O-LM cells are listed on Hippocampome.org.
Full-scale CA1: Bezaire et al. (2016) included OLM cells among their nine types and found that theta could be generated within CA1 itself, with specific roles for PV and OLM interneurons.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: An OLM-like population (slow, h-current-driven, targeting distal dendrites, excited by local principal cells) is how you get a theta-like rhythm and pathway switching in a model with two input streams.
A minimal theta-gamma model needs only three populations: pyramidal cells, fast PV-like basket cells and slow OLM-like cells with slow synapses.
In a cortical column model, the analogous population is the SST Martinotti cell (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cortical-interneurons/sst-martinotti).
